column6: The commentary's Noah scene includes a son who cannot shelter himself by lineage; Ezekiel names Noah among the righteous who could save only their own lives in a judged land, limiting the refuge righteousness provides.

The commentary notes lineage as a possible refuge but recounts Noah's son perishing; Ezekiel explicitly says even Noah could not deliver sons or daughters, making kinship no guarantee against judgment.
The commentary calls asr a shelter for the endangered; Boaz blesses Ruth for coming to take refuge under the wings of Israel's God, using the same protective image for a vulnerable outsider.
The commentary says a person's lineage can be a refuge; Ruth asks Boaz, her redeemer, to spread his wing over her, joining kinship protection to the sheltering image.

The commentary describes a calamity with no apparent exit and rescue from it; trapped Israel is told not to fear but to stand and see the Lord's salvation, making trust communal at the edge of danger.

column5: Israel crosses the sea on dry ground
column6: The commentary's Noah scene concerns water and a failed human refuge; Exodus says the people pass through the divided sea on dry ground, depicting deliverance as a path opened through the danger.
The commentary places a person in loss and peril; the psalm says the righteous have many afflictions but the Lord delivers them from all, joining endurance of trouble to rescue.
The commentary pictures people needing shelter and escape; sailors cry to the Lord in their trouble, and he stills the storm, making deliverance an answer to danger at sea.
The commentary's endangered person seeks safety; the psalm says God makes the storm a calm and its waves quiet, specifying the change from peril to safety.
The commentary names asr as a refuge and salvation place; the sailors are glad when the sea grows quiet and God brings them to their desired harbor, supplying a concrete destination for rescue.
The commentary joins clinging with rescue from a pit; the community says it escaped like a bird from a fowler's snare when the trap broke, an image of release from an inescapable-looking danger.

column5: children have refuge in fear of the Lord
column6: The commentary says lineage can be a refuge; Proverbs says the one who fears the Lord has strong confidence and his children have a refuge, locating family safety in trust in God.
The commentary mentions lineage as a sheltering root; the psalm says that even if father and mother forsake the speaker, the Lord will take him in, making divine refuge survive family failure.
The commentary develops refuge and armor as shelter; Moses calls the eternal God Israel's dwelling place with everlasting arms beneath, combining a safe home and protective arms.

column5: trust in the Lord as security
column6: The commentary identifies iman with entering safety; Jeremiah blesses the person who trusts in the Lord and makes the Lord his trust, stating the security relation directly.

column5: no fear in drought; still bears fruit
column6: The commentary joins faith, righteous action, and escape from loss; Jeremiah's tree planted by water has no fear when heat or drought comes and does not cease bearing fruit, linking trust to continued life and deeds.
The commentary describes the sabīr as one who stands with the group; Isaiah tells hearers to strengthen weak hands and steady feeble knees, making mutual support a response to fear.

column5: say to the fearful, God comes to save
column6: The commentary says people mutually counsel one another in truth and patience; Isaiah instructs them to tell anxious hearts to be strong because God comes to save, supplying the content and purpose of encouragement.

column5: refuge in rocky heights; sure provisions
column6: The commentary makes asr a shelter and armor a form of protection; Isaiah says the secure person dwells on heights, with rocky fortresses for refuge and bread and water assured.

column5: steadfast in a time of calamity
column6: The commentary associates sabr with calamity and endurance; Sirach tells the person serving God to set the heart right and be steadfast rather than panic in adversity.

column5: accept adversity; be patient in reversals
column6: The commentary records a branch sense of sabr as an ordeal with no exit; Sirach says to accept what comes and be patient when humbled, treating adversity as a test of fidelity.
The commentary calls iman security and sabr patience; Sirach joins trust, hope, and God's help, showing the expected refuge for a person enduring trial.

The commentary identifies believers with those who enter safety; a midrash commonly located at Genesis Rabbah 32:6 portrays Noah as hesitating until the waters press him into the ark, complicating that entry with a reading of delayed trust (the locator is from memory).

column5: Rahab's scarlet sign shelters her household
column6: The commentary joins a sheltering place, lineage, and clinging; 1 Clement retells Rahab's rescue by faith and hospitality, with a scarlet cord marking the house where her family is spared, making a household's refuge visible.

column5: tower as the Church and entry into it
column6: The commentary pictures a secure place reached by those who escape loss; Hermas's tower vision interprets the tower as the Church and distinguishes people by whether they can be built into it, giving the secure-community image an early Christian reading.

column5: we are perishing in the storm
column6: The commentary glosses khusr as perishing; the disciples in a storm wake Jesus with the fear that they are perishing, placing the word in a concrete scene of danger.

The commentary asks what shelter can save a person in danger; Jesus rebukes the wind and commands the sea to be still, and the storm ceases, presenting rescue from the peril named in the preceding verse.

column5: Peter cries, "save me" as he sinks
column6: The commentary describes a threatened person clinging for rescue; Peter begins to sink in the water and cries to Jesus to save him, making the appeal for refuge a physical scene.

column5: Jesus catches Peter; faith and doubt
column6: The commentary links iman with security; Jesus immediately catches Peter and names his little faith and doubt, showing rescue alongside a challenged trust.

column5: tribulation cannot separate believers from Christ's love
column6: The commentary places humanity in loss; Paul asks whether distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, or sword can separate those in Christ from his love, framing peril without surrender to loss.

column5: more than conquerors through the one who loves them
column6: The commentary's exception describes people who escape loss; Paul says believers prevail amid these dangers through the one who loves them, specifying the source of security.
The commentary glosses khusr as perishing; Paul includes death and life among powers unable to separate believers from God's love, offering a concrete Christian claim against ultimate loss.

column5: nothing can separate from God's love
column6: The commentary names iman as entry into safety; Paul's conclusion says no created thing can separate believers from God's love in Christ, making that safety comprehensive.
The commentary describes people in danger needing a refuge; Peter tells the community to cast all anxiety on God because he cares for them, making trust an act of placing burdens in protective hands.
The commentary joins patience with calamity; Peter says that after brief suffering God will restore, strengthen, and establish the believers, giving endurance an outcome of stability.

column5: God's household as pillar of truth
column6: The commentary calls truth what must be protected; Paul describes the Church as God's household and the pillar and foundation of truth, combining community and safeguarding the truth.
The commentary says al-haqq is what a person is obliged to protect; Timothy is told to guard the entrusted good deposit through the Holy Spirit, making protection of teaching explicit.
The commentary calls truth something to be guarded; Jude urges believers to contend for the faith once delivered to the saints, giving that protection a communal action.
The commentary links truth with what must be protected and shared; an overseer must hold fast the trustworthy word so he can exhort in sound teaching and refute contradiction.
The commentary says people mutually counsel one another in truth; Paul says love rejoices with the truth, placing truth inside the ethic governing a community.
The commentary joins truth and patience as communal virtues; Paul describes love as bearing and enduring all things, giving patience a shared ethical setting.
The commentary calls the sabīr one who stands with the group in its affairs; Paul tells believers to carry one another's burdens, describing that solidarity as fulfilling Christ's law.

column5: one member's suffering is shared by all
column6: The commentary describes a guarantor who stays with the community; Paul says when one member suffers, all suffer together, making communal presence concrete.

column5: Job's endurance and the Lord's compassion
column6: The commentary associates sabr with enduring calamity; James blesses those who endure and points to Job and the Lord's compassionate outcome, preserving both suffering and rescue.

column5: approach the throne for help in need
column6: The commentary calls asr a refuge for a person in distress; Hebrews invites people to approach the throne of grace to receive mercy and timely help, presenting access to God as refuge.
The commentary joins righteous action with truth; John says love must be shown in deed and truth rather than words alone, uniting the stanza's ethical features.

column5: labor in the Lord is not in vain
column6: The commentary says humanity is in loss and names righteous deeds; Paul urges steadfastness and abundant work because labor in the Lord is not empty, directly countering the fear that good action is lost.
The commentary says truth is what a person must protect; Peter tells believers to be ready to answer for their hope, with gentleness and respect, making public defense of faith a disciplined act.

column5: patient in tribulation; constant in prayer
column6: The commentary links sabr with calamity and the believers' refuge with iman; Paul summarizes communal life as rejoicing in hope, being patient in tribulation, and persevering in prayer.
